[Legal Basis for the Publication of the Budget Review and Outlook Paper]

The Budget Review and Outlook Paper is prepared in accordance with Section 26 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012.  The law states that:

The National Treasury shall prepare and submit to -Cabinet for approval, by the 30 th  September in each financial year, a Budget Review and Outlook Paper, which shall include:

Actual fiscal performance in the previous financial year compared to the budget appropriation for that year;

Updated macro-economic and financial forecasts with sufficient information to show changes from the forecasts in the most recent Budget Policy Statement

Information on how actual financial performance for the previous financial year may have affected compliance with the fiscal responsibility principles or the financial objectives in the latest Budget Policy Statement; and

The reasons for any deviation from the financial objectives together with proposals to address the deviation and the time estimated to do so.

Cabinet shall consider the Budget Review and Outlook Paper with a view to approving it, with or without amendments, not later than fourteen days after its submission.

Not later than seven days after the BROP has been approved by Cabinet, the National Treasury shall:

Submit the paper to the Budget Committee of the National Assembly to be laid before each house of Parliament; and

Publish and publicize the paper not later than fifteen days after laying the Paper before Parliament.

[Fiscal Responsibility Principles in the Public Finance Management Act]

In line with the Constitution, the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act, 2012, sets out the fiscal responsibility principles to ensure prudent and transparent management of public resources.  The PFM law (Section 15) states that:

Over the medium term, a minimum of 30% of the national budget shall be allocated to development expenditure

The national government's expenditure on wages and benefits for public officers shall not exceed a percentage of the national government revenue as prescribed by the regulations.

Over the medium term, the national government's borrowings shall be used only for the purpose of financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure

Public debt and obligations shall be maintained at a sustainable level as approved by Parliament (NG) and county assembly  (CG)

Fiscal risks shall be managed prudently

A reasonable degree of predictability with respect to the level of tax rates and tax bases shall be maintained, taking into account any tax reforms that may be made in the future

The less productive budgetary items have been rationalized downwards by between 20 to 75 percent.

This  macroeconomic  outlook  is  not  without  risks.  The  uncertainties  in  the  global  markets occasioned by the U.S. economic policies, the post-Brexit resolution, the pace of normalization of  monetary  policies  in  advanced  economies  and  the  recent  geopolitical  tensions  building around production and use of nuclear weapons are likely to weigh down global growth with negative impact on trade and financial flows.

Additionally,  the  economy  continues  to  be  exposed  to  adverse  weather  conditions  in  the medium term. Further, there are salary and recurrent expenditure pressures that continue to create fiscal risks. The Government will closely monitor these risks and undertake appropriate measures to safeguard macroeconomic stability should these risks materialize.

[Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper]

1. The objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper (BROP) is to provide a review of fiscal performance for the FY 2016/17 and how this performance impacts on the financial  objectives  and  fiscal  responsibility  principles  set  out  in  the  2017  Budget  Policy Statement  (BPS).  The  document  provides  highlights  of  recent  economic  developments  and outlook and sector ceilings for the FY 2018/19 budget and the medium term.

2. The sector ceilings are guided by the overall resource envelope that is informed by the macroeconomic and fiscal outlook as presented in section III and IV of this document. The sector ceilings set in motion the budget preparation for the FY 2018/19 and the medium term.

3. As required by the PFM Act, 2012, budget process aims to promote the efficient and effective use of resources, based on evidence and rational deliberation. To achieve this, the Government remains committed to a measured, prudent course of fiscal consolidation to narrow the budget deficit and stabilize debt.

[Objective of the 2017 Budget Review and Outlook Paper]

3. As required by the PFM Act, 2012, budget process aims to promote the efficient and effective use of resources, based on evidence and rational deliberation. To achieve this, the Government remains committed to a measured, prudent course of fiscal consolidation to narrow the budget deficit and stabilize debt.

4. In this  context,  the  2017  Budget  Policy  Statement  (BPS)  set  out  a  series  of macroeconomic policies, proposals to raise additional revenue and sustain core expenditure, improve value for money spent, stabilise the public finances, and contribute to economic growth and  employment  creation.  As  a  result  of  the  improved  fiscal  discipline  and  competent management of the economy, the macro-indicators for the FY 2017/18 are pointing in the right direction. The economy continues to register robust growth while macroeconomic stability is preserved.

5. To meet the current commitments as contained in the 2017/18 Budget, the Government proposed tax measures aimed at raising the tax revenue and providing incentives for industries to thrive and create employment opportunities.

6. However, the underperformance in both revenue collection and expenditure in the FY 2016/17 has implications on the financial objectives outlined in the 2017 BPS and the 2017/18 Budget. In particular, the baseline for projecting both the revenue and expenditures for the FY 2017/18 and the medium term has changed given the end FY 2016/17 and quarter one FY 2017/18 as well as the implications of the recent supplementary budget.

[C. Fiscal Performance for the FY 2016/17 in Relation to Financial Objectives]

30. The fiscal performance in the FY 2016/17 has affected the financial objectives set out in the 2017 BPS and the Budget for FY 2017/18 in the following ways:

The base for ordinary revenue projections is higher than the actual outcome by about Ksh 5.5 billion; as such there will be a downward base effect adjustment in ordinary revenues for FY 2017/18 and the medium term. This adjustment in revenues is expected to translate to a mix of downward adjustment in expenditure projections and upward adjustment in financing for the FY 2017/18. 56. On the domestic scene, the Kenyan economy has continued to experience challenges in 2017. 57. Given the above developments the growth outlook for 2017 has been revised down to 5.1 percent from 5.5 percent as earlier projected and 5.9 percent in the 2017 Budget Policy Statement (BPS). Similarly, the financial and insurance sector declined to 4.3 percent from 8.1 percent over the same period

[Inflation Rate]

Overall month on month inflation declined to 7.1 percent in September 2017 (within Government target range of 5+/-2.5 percent) from 8.0 percent in August 2017. The decline was due to fall in the cost of some food items which was mainly attributed to a relief from a situation of depressed supply of goods and services as experienced in August 2017. In the twelve month to September 2017, the average annual inflation rate was 8.4 percent compared to 6.5 percent in  the same period in 2016. Inflation is expected to decline and fall within the Government target range of 5+/-2.5 percent in the current fiscal year.

In the sub Saharan Africa region, the high inflation rates in Ghana and Nigeria reflect difficult economic conditions as a result of foreign currency shortages resulting from lower commodity revenues and slow policy adjustment. The low inflation in South Africa reflects improved weather conditions that led to a bumper crop harvest which resulted in lower food prices (Chart 2b). Closer home, the EAC region (except Burundi) continues to register low

Source of data: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics

inflation  rates  due  to  prudent  monetary  and  fiscal  policy  management.  Burundi  has  been experiencing high inflation rates due to recent drought and flooding episodes. Following this, the Burundi Government instituted customs measures on imported food that is stabilizing food prices in the country.

Source of data: National Central Banks

[Kenya Shilling Exchange Rate]

The Kenya Shilling exchange rate broadly remained stable against major international currencies.  In September 2017, against the dollar the Shilling depreciated by around 1.8 percent in nominal terms to close at Ksh 103.1from Ksh 101.3 in September 2016. Against the Euro and the Sterling pound, the Shilling weakened to Ksh 122.9 and Ksh 137.0 in  September 2017 from Ksh 113.5 and Ksh 133.2 in September 2016, respectively (Chart 3a).

As compared to the regional currencies, the Kenya Shilling exchange rate has continued to display relatively less volatility (Chart 3b). The stability of the Kenya shilling exchange rate reflected resilient receipts from tea and horticulture despite lower export volumes due to adverse

Source of data: Central Bank of Kenya

weather  conditions  in  the  first  quarter  of  2017.  Additionally,  receipts  from  tourism,  coffee exports and Diaspora remittances remained strong.

Source of data: Various National Central Banks

[Interest Rates]

Interest  rates  have  remained  fairly  low  and  stable.  The  Monetary  Policy Committee  at  their  meeting  of  18 th September  2017  left  the  Central  Bank  Rate unchanged at 10 percent. The interbank rate has remained low at 5.7 percent in September 2017 due to ample liquidity in the money market (Chart 4 ), while the 91-day Treasury bill rate declined to 8.1 percent in September from 8.6 percent in January 2017. The 182 day and the 364 day Treasury bills averaged 10.3 percent and 10.9 percent, respectively in September 2017.

The  interest  rate  spread  narrowed  to  6.3  percent  in  July  2017  from  11.2  percent  in August  2016 as  a  result  of  the  developments  in  the  lending  and  deposit  rates.  Commercial banks' average lending interest declined to 13.7 percent in July 2017 compared to 18.0 percent

Source of data: Central Bank of Kenya

in the first half of 2016. Meanwhile, the average commercial banks' deposit rate declined to 7.4 percent from 7.6 percent over the same period.

[Money Supply]

71. Growth of broad money supply, M3, improved to 8.3 percent in the year to July 2017 compared to a growth of 6.9 percent in the year to July 2016. The improved growth in the year to July 2017 was largely on account of an improvement in the uptake of domestic credit and growth of net foreign assets (NFA) of the Central Bank.

[Private Sector Credit]

72. Annual growth of credit to the private sector recorded a slight increase to 1.6 percent over the 12 months to August 2017 from 1.4 percent in July 2017, reversing the downward trend witnessed since August 2015. The real estate, manufacturing, trade, consumer durables and private households have continued on a net basis to receive credit flows from the banking sector since January 2017.

[External Sector Developments]

73. The overall balance of payments position improved to a deficit of US$ 65.9 million (0.1 percent of GDP) in the year to July 2017 from a deficit of US$ 1,252.9 million (2.0 percent of GDP) in the year to July 2016 (Chart 5). The current account balance was a deficit of US$ 4,384.8 million (5.8 percent of GDP) in the year to July 2017 from a deficit of US$ 3,141.6 million (4.9 percent of GDP) in the year to July 2016.

74. The deficit in the merchandise account widened reflecting increase in payments for import of oil on account of the rebound in international oil prices and the increase in imports of machinery and transport equipment mostly on account of imports of wagons, locomotives and associated equipment related to the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) project.  In  addition,  net  export  of  goods  and  services  declined  on  account  of  lower exports of goods (mainly horticulture, oil products, manufactured goods, chemicals and related products). Inflows to the services account increased by 0.3 percent as a result of improvement in the travel services in line with the recovery in tourist arrivals.

[External Sector Developments]

74. The deficit in the merchandise account widened reflecting increase in payments for import of oil on account of the rebound in international oil prices and the increase in imports of machinery and transport equipment mostly on account of imports of wagons, locomotives and associated equipment related to the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) project.  In  addition,  net  export  of  goods  and  services  declined  on  account  of  lower exports of goods (mainly horticulture, oil products, manufactured goods, chemicals and related products). Inflows to the services account increased by 0.3 percent as a result of improvement in the travel services in line with the recovery in tourist arrivals.

75. The flows in the Financial Account increased to US$ 6,541.2 million in July 2017 compared with US$ 3,590.9 million in July 2016. The financial inflows were mainly in the form of direct investment and other investment which stood at US$ 135 million and US$ 7,023 million, respectively in July 2017. Other investment inflows mainly include foreign financing for Government infrastructure projects.

Source of data: Central Bank of Kenya

[Foreign Exchange Reserves]

76. The  banking  system's  foreign  exchange  holdings  increased  to  US$  10,550 million in July 2017 from US$ 10,381 million in July 2016 (Chart 6). This was due to the increased holdings by commercial banks to US$ 2,415 million in 2017 from US$ 2,217 million in 2016. The official foreign exchange reserves held by the Central Bank remained strong at US$ 8,135 million (5.4 months of import cover) in July 2017 compared with US$ 8,165 million (5.3 months of import cover) in July 2016.

Source of data: Central Bank of Kenya

[Developments in the Capital Markets]

77. There has been a gradual recovery in the activities  of the capital markets  beginning February 2017.  The NSE 20 Share Index improved to 3,751 points in September 2017 from 2,995 points in February 2017 while the market capitalization improved to Ksh 2,377 billion from Ksh 1,825 billion over the same period, a reflection of investor confidence in the economy.

[Global Growth Outlook]

78. Global economy is on a recovery path with the growth expected to pick up to 3.5 percent in 2017 from 3.2 percent in 2016, supported by the recovery of manufacturing and trade, rising investor confidence, favorable global financing conditions, and stabilizing commodity prices.

79. Growth  in  advanced  economies  remains  subdued  reflecting  the  macroeconomic implications of changes in policy assumptions though improving conditions in a number of the euro countries is expected to raise global economic activity. Growth in emerging market and developing economies are projected to see a sustained pick up from 4.3 percent in 2016 to 4.6 percent in 2017 and 4.8 percent in 2018, primarily driven by gradually improving conditions in large  commodity  exporters  that  experienced  recessions  in  2015-16,  caused  by  declining commodity prices.

80. The economic growth in the sub-Saharan African (SSA) region is expected to pick up in 2017 to 2.7 percent from 1.3 percent in 2016 supported by positive growth prospects for South Africa (one of the largest economies in Sub-Saharan Africa), which is experiencing a bumper crop due to better rainfall and an increase in mining output prompted by a moderate rebound in commodity prices. In the East African Community (EAC) region, economic growth is projected to pick up in 2017 supported by ongoing infrastructure investment efforts, strong private consumption and the lower global oil prices.

[Domestic Growth Outlook]

81. On the domestic scene, the Kenyan economy has continued to experience challenges in 2017 particularly the negative impact of the severe drought that started in 2016, the prolonged electioneering period that culminated in the August 2017 General elections and the repeat of the Presidential Election slated for October 2017, as well as the subdued credit growth to the private  sector  have  combined  to  weaken  growth.  These  developments  have  resulted  in uncertainties among investors, business community and consumers as they adopt a wait and see attitude, thus weighing down the growth outlook.

82. Given the above developments the growth outlook for 2017 has been revised down to 5.1 percent from 5.5 percent as earlier projected and 5.9 percent in the 2017 Budget Policy Statement (BPS).

83. Going forward in terms of fiscal years, the economic growth is projected at 6.5 percent in  the  FY  2018/19  and  7.1  percent  over  the  medium  term  supported  by  improved  global conditions, improved production in agriculture, ongoing recovery of tourism and completion of key public projects in roads, rail and energy generation, resilient exports and benefits from ongoing regional integration efforts. In addition, the strong consumer demand and private sector investment as well as a stable macroeconomic environment in the country will help reinforce this growth.

[Domestic Growth Outlook]

83. Going forward in terms of fiscal years, the economic growth is projected at 6.5 percent in  the  FY  2018/19  and  7.1  percent  over  the  medium  term  supported  by  improved  global conditions, improved production in agriculture, ongoing recovery of tourism and completion of key public projects in roads, rail and energy generation, resilient exports and benefits from ongoing regional integration efforts. In addition, the strong consumer demand and private sector investment as well as a stable macroeconomic environment in the country will help reinforce this growth.

84. The growth projections over the medium term are aligned to those of the Medium Term Plan  II  (2013-2017)  and  those  in  its  successor  Medium  Term  Plan  III  (2018-2022)  that  are implementing Vision 2030 (Table 10 and Annex Table 1).

[Monetary Policy Outlook]

Overall month on month inflation remained above target in the first half of 2017 peaking at 11.7 percent in May 2017 mainly due to increased prices of food following the prolonged drought. In subsequent months, inflation declined falling within target in September 2017. This followed reduced prices of food items after weather conditions improved in the second quarter of the year and measures taken by the government to temporary exempt import on maize, sugar and powdered milk.

The continued prudent monetary policy measures coupled with the expected favourable weather outlook and the policy interventions  on food imports will moderate demand-driven inflationary pressures. Further, the stability of the Kenya exchange rate will reinforce the price stability  objective  and  keep  inflation  within  the  Government  target  range  in  the  remainder period of the fiscal year and in the medium term.

The main risks to inflation remain adverse weather that affects agricultural production and their prices, and potential volatility in international oil prices.

The close coordination of fiscal and monetary policies will continue to delivering on price stability and reduction in cost of doing business in the country.

[External Sector Outlook]

Kenya's international trade is estimated to grow in volume terms with improvements in weather conditions improving earnings from our exports of tea, coffee and horticulture exports. Further,  with  diversification  of  Kenya's  export  products  and  access  to  other  international

markets, Kenya's exports are expected to improve over the medium term. It is also expected that oil prices will remain stable, diaspora remittances resilient and strong receipts from tourism. These developments will support a relatively narrow current account deficit over the medium term and strengthen the Kenya's external position thereby reinforcing stability in the Kenya Shilling exchange rate. In addition, IMF precautionary Arrangement facility of approximately US$ 1,500 million  is  expected  to  provide  additional  buffer  against  short  term  external  and domestic shocks.

[Fiscal Policy Outlook]

90. Fiscal policy over the medium-term aims at supporting rapid and inclusive economic growth, ensuring a sustainable debt position by narrowing the budget deficit and at the same time supporting the devolved system of Government for effective delivery of services.

91. Over the medium term revenue collection is expected to rise to about 19.4 percent of GDP by FY 2020/21 while expenditures will decline gradually from 26.8 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18 to 24.4 percent of GDP in FY 2020/21. As a result, the overall budget deficit inclusive of grants is projected to decline to 4.6 percent of GDP in the medium term from 8.9 percent in FY 2016/17.

[D. Risks to the Domestic Economic Outlook]

92. This  macroeconomic  outlook  is  not  without  risks.  The  uncertainties  in  the  global markets  occasioned  by  the  U.S.  economic  policies,  the  post-Brexit  resolution,  the  pace  of normalization of monetary policies in advanced economies and the recent geopolitical tensions building around production and use of nuclear weapons are likely to weigh down global growth with negative impact on trade and financial flows.

93. The Kenyan economy in 2017, is experiencing the impacts of a prolonged electoral process that has created uncertainty amongst investors, business community and consumers and has potential adverse impact on tourism and security amongst others, weighing down the growth outlook for 2017.

94. Additionally, the economy continues to be exposed to adverse weather conditions in the medium term. Further, there are salary and recurrent expenditure pressures that continue to create fiscal risks.

95. The Government will closely monitor these risks and undertake appropriate measures to safeguard macroeconomic stability should these risks materialize.

[A. Adjustments to the FY 2017/18 Budget]

96. As preparations for the FY 2018/19 medium-term budget commence, it is worth noting that the implementation of the FY 2017/18 budget is experiencing challenges particularly on revenue  collection  and  elevated  expenditure  pressures.  The  adverse  spillover  effects  of  the prolonged  drought,  the  repeat  of  Presidential  Election  scheduled  for  October  2017,  salary shortfalls and the under performance of the main revenue tax heads are some of the challenges that have led to the revision of the FY 2017/18 budget.

97. As such the revenue forecasts for FY 2017/18 have been reviewed downwards to reflect outcome  in  FY  2016/17  and  also  taking  into  account  the  fiscal  developments  through  end September 2017. Further, expenditure projections have been revised to accommodate some of these challenges, emerging priorities and provide room for salary shortfalls under the recently approved supplementary budget I. These additional expenditures have been accommodated by tradeoffs and reallocations of the existing budgetary provisions supported by austerity measures instituted  on  less  productive  areas  of  spending  across  the  Government.  The  less  productive budgetary items have been rationalized downwards by between 20 to 75 percent in order to accommodate the additional expenditure priorities and to ensure a sustainable fiscal profile that supports economic expansion and sustainable debt position.

[B. Medium Term Fiscal Projections]

98. Over the medium term, driven by continued reforms, revenue collection is expected to rise to about 19.4 percent of GDP by FY 2020/21 (Annex Tables 2 and 3) . Overall expenditures will decline gradually from 26.8 percent of GDP in FY 2017/18 to 24.4 percent of GDP in FY 2020/21. Overall recurrent expenditures are expected to decline from 16.3 percent of GDP in FY  2017/18  to  14.4  percent  in  the  medium  term  while  development  and  net  lending expenditures is projected at 6.9 percent of GDP over the medium term.

99. The overall budget deficit inclusive of grants is projected to decline to 4.6 percent of GDP in the medium term, as major infrastructural projects currently being implemented by the Government  are  completed.  This  will  reinforce  policy  of  consistency  and  predictability  of government spending and will be achieved through the following strategies:

 Directing more resources coming from enhanced revenue collection to development related activities as we curtail recurrent spending;

 Ensuring efficient and effective public spending; and

 Ensuring that capital expenditure proposals have been thoroughly scrutinized  and prioritized so that only high impact projects are accommodated using scarce resources.

[C. FY 2018/19 Budget Framework]

100. The  FY  2018/19  budget  framework  is  intended  to  continue  the  fiscal  consolidation agenda with the completion of SGR phase I, shedding off election related expenditures, drought related interventions and other one offs expenditure programmes, particularly those related to security. The overall fiscal deficit including grants is expected to decline from 8.9 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17 to 5.9 percent in FY 2018/19. This consolidation will bolster our debt

sustainability position and give flexibility for counter cyclical fiscal policy interventions when appropriate.

101. Revenue Projections: In the FY 2018/19 revenue collection including Appropriationin-Aid (AiA) is projected to increase to Ksh 1,882.5 billion (18.8 percent of GDP) up from Ksh 1,647.2 billion (18.7 percent of GDP) in the FY 2017/18. This revenue performance will be underpinned by on-going reforms in tax policy and revenue administration. Ordinary revenues will amount to Ksh 1,717.0 billion (17.2 percent of GDP) in FY 2018/19 up from Ksh 1,490.4 billion (16.9 percent of GDP) in FY 2017/18.

107. Transfer to County Governments: With Ordinary revenue projections slightly rising from 17.0 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17 to FY 17.2 percent of GDP in the FY 2018/19, and at the same time expenditures under the Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) increasing from 4.8 percent of GDP in FY 2016/17 to 7.5 percent of GDP in FY 2018/19, each level of Government is expected to broadly support the fiscal consolidation. In this respect therefore, the National Government  expenditures  funded  from  domestic  resources  are  projected  to  decline  by  1.5 percent of GDP. Similarly the allocation to County Governments is projected to decline by 0.2 percent of GDP, from 3.5 percent in FY 2017/18 to 3.3 percent in FY 2018/19. The nominal year-on-year growth of allocation to the county governments is projected to remain stable at about 7 percent.

 Social Protection, Culture & Recreation - resources to double the number of vulnerable citizens  supported  through  the  cash  transfer  programme  (Inua  Jamii);  and  provision  of health insurance cover through the NHIF for all citizens above the age of 70. [V. CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS]

111. The  FY  2018/19  and  the  Medium  Term  budget  and  fiscal  framework  projections presented  in  this  BROP  takes  into  account  the  expected  strong  domestic  growth  due  to  the recovery in the global economy, continued public infrastructure investment, enhanced revenue collection following improved  tax  administration as well  as  a  stable  macroeconomic environment.  It  also  takes  into  account  risks  facing  economy  such  as  public  expenditures pressures which may reallocate resources from the productive sectors.

112. As  such,  the  fiscal  strategy  in  this  BROP  will  focus  on  enhancing  overall  revenue collection  and  reallocating  resources  to  productive  sectors  of  the  economy.  The  strategy therefore,  targets  to  maintain  fiscal  discipline  in  all  levels  of  the  government  for  maximum return from public resources in line with the Fiscal Responsibility Principles outlined in the PFM law.

113. Going forward, the set of policies outlined in this BROP ensures continuity in resource allocation  based  on  prioritized  programs  that  have  been  earmarked  by  the  government  to accelerate growth, employment creation and poverty reduction.
